utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Defence wanted to raise a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Only a short thing. I just spoke with the Prosecution. We would just ask for an additional 20 minutes for direct with this witness, so it would be 50 minutes in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are. Mr. Milorad Bukva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile I use the time to deal with one matter, and it has got to do with Witness Keserovic. From the 17th to the 19th of June of last year, Witness Keserovic testified before this Chamber as a Prosecution fact witness. On the 19th of May of this year, the Defence filed its Rule 65 ter witness list which included Witness Keserovic. On the 23rd of May, following inquiries made by the Chamber as to why Prosecution witnesses were included on a Defence witness list, the Defence made submissions that it intended to call Witness Keserovic to provide further testimony. You can find this at transcript pages 21427 to 21429, and 21586 to 21587. The Chamber interpreted the Defence's submissions in its witness list and in court as a request to recall the witness for further cross-examination. On the 3rd of June, 2014, the Prosecution responded to the Defence's request not opposing the proposed recall. However, on the 27th of August, the Defence informed the Chamber that it is unlikely that it will want to recall Witness Keserovic and that the Defence is looking for a replacement witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber therefore, without prejudice, hereby dismisses the Defence request to recall Witness Keserovic as moot and strikes him from the Defence witness list. Good morning, Mr. Bukva.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not very polite to continue with other things when you entered the courtroom. Apologies for that. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We didn't hear any interpretation. Now I can imagine, more or less, what the interpretation would have been.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Wrong channel. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we then hear the interpretation although ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Bukva. We had a little problem with the translation. If you would have any problem in hearing in your own language what is said, please draw my attention to that. Mr. Bukva, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bukva.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For the record, will you please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: My name is Milorad Bukva.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now pull up in e-court 1D1724. This is Mr. Bukva's statement. I also submitted a hard copy of this statement. And if the usher would be so kind to hand one to the Prosecution first for them to ascertain that it's a clean copy. [In English] I left it with the -- already with them. So just be shown to the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bukva, you have it both on the screen and on paper, the first page of this document. Do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the statement before you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you provide that statement to the Defence team of Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the last page, now. [In English] We should have -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see it also on the screen. Do you recognise the signature on the last page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes. It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you the same questions today, would you answer the same as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, is this statement accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes. It is accurate and everything in it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender at this moment the statement of Mr. Bukva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1724 will be Exhibit D608.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would -- I would just read now a summary statement, with your leave. Thank you. As a professional soldier, Milorad Bukva will speak about his education and military duties he performed. He will present his observations regarding the inter-ethnic situation in Sarajevo before and after the multiparty elections, about the Muslims organising into paramilitary groups, about the organised criminal attacks on the JNA facilities, personnel and their families, and about the pullout of the JNA units from Sarajevo. Milorad Bukva will testify about the establishing of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and its composition. He will present information about the 1st Corps of the Muslim army of B and H and about the forces of that corps in Sarajevo. Milorad Bukva will speak about the constant fire by Muslim forces from all neighbourhoods of Sarajevo, about the sniper fire and sniper nests. He will also testify about continuous abuse of the Red Cross emblem by the members of the 1st Corps of the ABiH and about the 1st Corps opening artillery fire from the hospital perimeter, the health centre, schools, and kindergartens. He will also present information about the camps for Serbs, about the killings and constant abuse of the Serbs, the sexual abuse of Serb women, their being prevented to leave the city, et cetera. I don't know if something is wrong, but I'm not receiving English translation at this spot. I don't know if everybody else is okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's because you are talking in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe that's why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Milorad Bukva will also testify as to what the UNPROFOR personnel stated regarding Markale 1 and Markale 2 at the meetings he attended himself. Further, he will testify about General Mladic's comportment towards war prisoners and civilian population and his attitude towards the Serb paramilitaries. He will speak about General Mladic as a person and a leader. Mr. Bukva will also present information about the number of family members murdered during World War II and about the Serb mass graves in Dubica and its surroundings, where he comes from. That was the short summary and I will, with your leave, Your Honours, have some questions for Mr. Bukva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For that purpose, at the beginning we'll need 1D3629. It's a map Mr. Bukva marked in Galic case. We'll -- we uploaded different map since this one is not the right one. So I'll probably have to come back. I'll continue and try to solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning. I believe that the correct map has a different 65 ter number, if I -- I think that it's at 1D3093. That should be the correct map.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have then -- yes, that's the map we are looking for. Then we will have to correct Mr. Bukva's statement in paragraph 20. Now in -- just for the record, since Mr. Bukva does not know the numbers, he just knows the map shown to him, then in paragraph 20 instead of "65 ter 1D3629," it should be put "1D3093." And I want to thank to my learned friend for her help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then the witness has a hard copy of his statement with him. Could you look at paragraph 20 of the hard copy and could you look at the map which is on your screen. And could you tell us whether what you referred to in paragraph 20 is what is marked on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is this map. But what we see on the screen is only one half of the map. There is another half.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the next page of the same document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. What we have on our screen now is the first -- no, what we have on our screen now is the second page which is the city centre of Sarajevo rather than what we saw on page 1 of this document; page 1 mainly dealing with the western part, including Dobrinja, of Sarajevo. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You are right. So this document has to be understood that the second page is actually the right part of the first page. They should be connected in that way. That's the right part then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unfortunately we have now twice the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record and to understand this map that you marked, Mr. Bukva, in the Galic case, would you just tell us what these abbreviations or acronyms mean? We see KM, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: It's the usual sign for the command post of a certain unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is Lpbr?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: That's the acronym for light infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is R?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: R is how I marked locations where weapons and ammunition were manufactured.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about N?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: N is a designation for weapons and ammunitions depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: TN?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: TN means locations where heavy weaponry was deployed and concentrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose units did you mark on this map?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Enemy units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that we don't go through them one by one, because one whole day in the Galic case was spent marking this map, only tell us what the numbers on this map mean; for instance, 142nd Lpbr?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: That's the establishment name of the unit. In this case 142nd Light Infantry Brigade. Or this flag in the shape of a square, inside it's written "1.K," it means the 1st Corps. I should just like to emphasize that these were the chief targets we identified in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps of the BH Army. There were many more, of course. But these were the main ones and the most interesting to our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On this map -- for instance, you mentioned 1K, the 1st Corps. Is that the command or the units of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: That was the command post of the 1st Corps, and in this specific case it is located at the address Danijel Ozma Street number 2, and that was across the street from the building of the Presidency. The place where the command of the 1st Corps was was a residential building, and its basement was used for the requirements of the command of the 1st Corps while the rest of the building was still occupied by local residents, the same people who lived there before the war, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it normal for the commands of the units of the BH Army to be placed in civilian facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: That was practically a rule. I would just like to say that two or three units were located in the prewar barracks of the former JNA. All the other Muslim units used buildings of a similar type like the one that was used for the 1st Corps command. This was something that the Muslims resorted to often and, like I said, it could be considered a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what were your duties? Could you please tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: When the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was formed after a decision of the Assembly of Republika Srpska of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it was called before, on the 12th of May, 1992, I was appointed chief of intelligence and security corps part -- as part of the intelligence and security department of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And that was my post throughout the entire period, with the formation of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps until the signing of the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And could you please tell us, what were your duties? What was your organ doing?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: My department that I led was assigned with gathering information of all kinds, but the focus was information about the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So my department mostly dealt with gathering information about the enemy, about the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the so-called armija. Of course, we gathered different kinds of information, too, about the general situation in the field, about the relations within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the morale, the weapons that the army had, their plans, their objectives, movements, regrouping of the forces, and all the things that are important from the security aspect, a high level of security as far as our units were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this gathering of intelligence, did that also include the positions of the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The most complete answer to your question would precisely be the last thing that I said. Everything that was important regarding the enemy, everything that was important and that could affect the security of our armed forces and our civilian population that was in the combat zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us what the sources of your information were?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: We used various sources for information. Most frequently, reconnaissance of enemy communications, then conversations or interviews of people who switched to the other side or who escaped from territories under Muslim control, by monitoring the media, enemy media, by direct reconnaissance on lines of contact, by sending our reconnaissance units into the depth of enemy territory, information coming from settlements. That would be more or less it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when you listen to enemy communications, were you able to anticipate enemy actions? Do you have any examples for that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: There are many, many examples of that. At the Slobodan Princip Seljo barracks, which was a former JNA barracks, we formed a listening centre by apparatus that we had at hand with just some professional devices, and we were able to successfully monitor enemy communications traffic, particularly at the beginning of the war. And so I can immediately give you an example from the beginning of the war. War had not officially broken out yet, but this was an attack on a JNA column in Dobrovoljacka Street. I just happened to be there when Izetbegovic, from Lukavica, where he was brought from the airport, informed Ganic in a telephone conversation about the plan of the withdrawal of the command from Bistrik. And then after that telephone conversation when Ganic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you tell us who was supposed to pull out?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The command from Bistrik under the command of General Kukanjac. So after that conversation, Izetbegovic and Ganic continued the conversation and chaos broke out in the enemy communications. We could clearly hear different armed groups calling to each other and openly calling for Osa and Zolja weapons to be brought, everything that they had that was available to them of weaponry. On the basis of that communication, it was quite clear that the column in Dobrovoljacka Street would be attacked, and this is what did happen. For some eight to ten minutes of that conversation on enemy communications lines, I actually told General Djurdevic [as interpreted] about those eight to ten minutes of communication, and General Gagovic also, who at that time was in Lukavica. I was disappointed when General Djurdjevac just commented on that by saying, "Bukva, we have guarantees from Mr. Doyle and the UNPROFOR commander that the process of the pullout of the command from Bistrik would proceed without any incidents." Unfortunately, my assumptions turned out to be correct and there was a massacre that took place in Dobrovoljacka Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, could I ask you a question. The Chamber has heard some evidence about the events in the Dobrovoljacka Street but not, as far as I remember, from the preceding communications within the federation circles. Now when you listened into this communication, was it -- first, was it recorded; second, was it transcribed in one way or another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The audio that I talked about was recorded and it's somewhere in the archives. I don't know exactly what happened to the recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the parties whether any effort was made to trace such recordings? Because, Mr. Lukic, often when the Prosecution relies on intercepted communications, they often come with audio and transcriptions. Is there any underlying audio or are there any underlying transcripts or have you searched for them or have you sought the co-operation of the Prosecution to find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We did talk with Mr. Bukva about that, and we couldn't locate those intercepts. But I think that maybe the next question can put a bit more light on this, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I'll wait for that. But you did not speak with the Prosecution about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bukva, you said that this should be somewhere in the archives. Did this archive remain in Republika Srpska or did the JNA take it with you when it withdrew to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, the archive is in Republika Srpska. The last place where I know it was located was the Vrbas barracks in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this communication took place on the same day that the attack happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you something else. We will try to get to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I nevertheless ask one or two follow-up questions. You said the last place where you know it was located was the Vrbas barracks in Banja Luka. When was it that you know that it was located there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was on the 8th of March, 2007, when I was demobilised from the Army of Republika Srpska. That was the last day of my active military service and the last day that I know that the archive was at the Vrbas barracks in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do I then understand that, if I could say so, that control over these archives has always been in Republika Srpska hands and not in federation hands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that is correct. It was always in our possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask the Prosecution to try to find out whether any such a collection of audio is known to it, either in audio or in transcription. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bukva, one follow-up question about this. Today do you have to ask permission from the Defence Ministry of Bosnia Herzegovina in order to have access to anything that is located at the Kozara barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, that was a rule already when I was still in active military service. Right after the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia Herzegovina was formed, as well as all the other joint defence organs, everything that had to do with the archives and other military issues was directly in the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the archive in this case. That was also treated in the same way. As far as I know, these rules are still in force today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would briefly like to put some questions to you about the departure of the JNA and the forming of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. When the JNA left the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what did that lead to, their departure from the territory?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The departure of the JNA from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was a political decision reached or respected fully by the military leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in an attempt to contribute to a peaceful resolution of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have to say that the Yugoslav People's Army in the period before the interethnic conflicts broke out was a significant factor of stability in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I have proof of that. At least on two occasions, and perhaps even three, the civilian population asked to be allowed to go into the barracks where I served, Slobodan Princip Seljo, in Lukavica, and when they came I spoke to those people, among whom were Serbs, Muslims, Croats, about their fears which grew from day-to-day for the simple reason that armed groups of Muslims began to appear in the Dobrinja settlement. These groups were headed by well-known Sarajevo criminals, such as Juka Prazina, Musan Topalovic, Caco, Ismet Bajramovic, Celo, and so on and so forth. And this caused fear among the civilian population, and they sought safety in the compound of the barracks where I was serving. I repeat: This happened twice, perhaps even three times. I don't remember exactly. This in itself indicates that the people trusted the JNA. The political decision that I referred to led to a situation, a political situation, of complete differentiation along ethnic lines because with the departure of the JNA, the people understood that something that they had faith in until the day before had disappeared, and it was clear that hard times were coming. So everybody followed the principle: I'm going to where my people are a majority. This led to demographic shifts among ethnic lines, and already at that time it was known, this truth was becoming evident among the people, that war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was inevitable. I have to emphasize that the greatest disappointment with the departure of the JNA was felt among the Serbian people, because the Serb people were traditionally committed to the JNA and they always supported the army. The fact that the JNA left the territory created the need to respond in an adequate manner to Muslim and Croat preparations for what was about to happen, and the Serb people self-organised, created armed groups, and then later they formed the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we have little time left and a lot to cover. Could you just, please, give me briefer answers. Tell us, briefly, what was the first time when you met General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date when I first met General Ratko Mladic, and that's understandable, but I know it was after the decision of Republika Srpska to establish its army and after the departure of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina. I know that for a fact because I clearly remember the situation when I met General Ratko Mladic. It was in the building of the command of the unit I served in, the 351st Communications Regiment, Signals Regiment. And since I was the only one from that unit left in Lukavica, I met the general in the hallway of that building and suggested to him to occupy the office of my former commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why were you left there alone? Where were the others from your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: With the withdrawal of the JNA, my unit, the 351st Signals Regiment of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, left with all the other troops to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I, as a native of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had expressed my desire to stay there and my commander did not have a problem with it. I also have to stress that the Muslims left the Yugoslav People's Army, I mean officers and non-commissioned officers who are Muslim, took place after the JNA decided to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina. Muslim officers and non-commissioned officers were until that moment part of the JNA and after that they left the JNA. Out of an approximate number of 120 officers and NCOs in my unit, approximately two or three of us remained. And another noteworthy thing to say in view of certain misinterpretations concerns the assets that were left behind: One rifle with one combat set, that's 150 rounds; one pistol; two hand-grenades, and that was it. All the rest was taken by the unit to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one helmet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you ask the witness to give short answers focussed on your question, then you should stop him at the point where he moves away from your question rather than to -- it's you who --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, although --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- is in control of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva covered several next questions. I wanted to ask about the assets left behind after the withdrawal of JNA. But thank you. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bukva, we really have to stream-line this from now on. So from which units was the Army of Republika Srpska established? Especially the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: After the departure of the JNA, the VRS was formed of the units that remained on the ground along territorial lines, and we used them to form as much as possible the VRS and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Those were these troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, when did the Army Republika Srpska become operative?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: It went very slowly because the decision was taken on the 12th of May, 1992. It took a long time to do that job because it's a process, a time-consuming one. But at any rate, at the end of 1992 you could call it an army, an organised army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to ask you something about the Muslim side now. Who were the leaders of the Patriotic League? To whom did the Patriotic League belong? What kind of information did your service obtain?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The Patriotic League was the militant wing of the SDA. It was the prime mover of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Hardened criminals in Sarajevo were used for that purpose. It was enough to give them weapons to know that an armed conflict would ensue. The political leadership of the SDA was fully aware, and it was done with complete awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did your service gain any information about the existence of prisons in Sarajevo for Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Within the general range of issues that we collected information on, we also had information about these prison locations, but our information was incomplete and many of them remained undetected until the end of the war because some of them were private prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you observed the enemy, tell us if the enemy attacked Serb positions and how often?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: That happened very often. The Sarajevo theatre of war was known as one with daily activity, and in these offensive operations it was the Muslim forces that were active, even during cease-fires. The intensity of combat operations did not change even during cease-fires. Cease-fires were observed only briefly by the Muslim side and very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Serbs have an interest in maintaining cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Absolutely. I must stress that the Serbs had never even thought about war before. Serb people had a very strong desire for a peaceful solution to the Bosnia-Herzegovina issue, and their hope that the war would stop never died because the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, by the end of 1943 [as interpreted], was exhausted by combat. We observed strictly every cease-fire agreement and we had strict orders from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's a break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, I specifically did not call a break because you are three minutes off from your 50 minutes, so therefore I thought you would finish and then we take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll then have shortly to go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, did your service obtain any information as to whether Muslim forces used hospitals, schools, et cetera, from which to open fire?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, we can see it on the map. There are several locations that confirm this. For instance, primary school -- I don't see very well the name of the school, but one battalion of the 102nd Brigade was in the Pavle Goranin primary school. We have already discussed the command post of the 1st Corps. For instance, also at Hrid, there was a battalion of the 115th Infantry Brigade. Then the weapons workshop at Marin Dvor was located in a machine engineering school. Or the detachment Djerzelez was located at Dobrinja in a kindergarten.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bukva. We have no further questions at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Bukva, we'll take a break. After the break, you'll be cross-examined by Ms. MacGregor. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I would briefly deal with a videolink matter. On the 27th of August, the Defence has filed a motion to hear the testimony of a witness via videolink but erroneously gave two dates of testimony: First week of September, and the week of the 22nd of September. The Chamber understands the reference to the first week of September to be a mistake and considers the request to relate to the week of the 22nd of September. And that's the reason why we would like to confirm with the Defence that this interpretation is correct, and I saw that you were nodding yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not the most reliable source on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And if you allow me to check with my case manager, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if our reading is correct in considering the time needed to facilitate such a request, the Chamber would like to ask the Prosecution if it could already indicate when a response can be expected. We'll hear from you later, Ms. Bibles. Ms. MacGregor, if you're ready to start your cross-examination. Mr. Bukva, you'll be cross-examined by Ms. MacGregor. Ms. MacGregor is counsel for the Prosecution. But before we start, Mr. Lukic had something to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I forgot, Your Honours, to offer associated exhibits into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First in general terms, any objections against associated exhibits announced?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll deal with that in a minute, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's not make the witness further wait for us to deal with administrative matters. We'll, at the end of this session, deal with the associated exhibits. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Bukva. A few preliminaries. You were --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You were a witness for the defence in General Galic's trial at this Tribunal in 2003; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: During that trial you testified for three days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, on your visit to The Hague this time, can you tell us when you arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: This time I arrived on Tuesday. I was here at 8.00 in the evening. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So today being Monday, you've been here almost a week.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And did you follow the testimony of the Defence witness who preceded you, Velimir Dunjic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Partially, yes. Partially. On the internet.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did you speak with Mr. Dunjic after his testimony finished?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him afterwards. He left. I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm going to move on now to some general questions about the structure of the SRK intelligence section that you were posted to. Starting in May 1992, is it correct that you worked in the SRK section for intelligence and security affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct, but it's correct that it wasn't sector, section, but department. It had two departments: The security department and the intelligence department, and the chief of the department was one person. The chief of the security department was at the same time the chief of the security intelligence affairs of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Who is the chief that you're now referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The chief of the department for security and intelligence affairs of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was at that time Lieutenant-Colonel Lugonja, and he was the head of that department during the whole war. So I -- I was the chief of the -- both intelligence and security departments of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and he was my superior along that line of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I want to make sure that the record doesn't become confused with the word "section," "department," et cetera, especially because it's possible some of it is lost in translation. So to be clear, Colonel Marko Lugonja was the chief of the SRK section for intelligence and security affairs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And you worked directly under him as the chief of the intelligence department at the corps level?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, I think you also just said that you were also the chief of the security department underneath Colonel Lugonja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, no. I'm going to be completely precise. The department for security and intelligence affairs of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps comprised two entities, two departments: One for intelligence - and I was the chief of that department; the other one was for security affairs, and the chief of that department was Lieutenant-Colonel Lugonja at the time. But the chief of the security intelligence affairs was the chief of the department of security, Lieutenant-Colonel Lugonja. So do you understand that? Those -- the chief was Lugonja of those both departments and he was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. It may help to explain, if you can answer, as you were the chief of the intelligence affairs, who was the chief of the security affairs also underneath Colonel Lugonja?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Lugonja was performing two functions. He was the chief of the intelligence security department and at the same time the chief of the security department. I was the chief of the intelligence department, and let me just add that I was also his deputy. In his absence I stood in for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Did you also have colleagues Marinko Milidrag and Brane Lubura?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, they were in the department. I have to say that we lacked manpower as far as cadre was concerned because we focused on lower-ranking organisational units to bring them up to full complement. So besides Marinko and Lubura, we also had Zoran Kos who was in charge of some administrative affairs. As for professional duties, we had Lugonja, he was the chief, there was me, Milidrag, and Lubura.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: As a member of the SRK intelligence staff, is it correct that Colonel Lugonja had two chains of command that he was required to report up?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, you couldn't put it that way. There are no two chains of command. The department for security and intelligence was an organisational unit of the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, but it was an element by establishment of that command. And so in the command it was subordinated to the corps command, in the command and disciplinary aspect. But in the professional aspect, our department was subordinated to the administration -- to the security administration of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska Army. So the chief of the department was not - let me put it that way - subordinated to the corps commander in the professional sense, I repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I may have confused the question by talking about two chains of command. To simplify it, on some matters Colonel Lugonja was required to report directly to the SRK corps command, and on other matters he was required to report directly to the VRS Main Staff intelligence structure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No. In the professional sense, Colonel Lugonja reported exclusively to his superior command along the professional line; i.e., the security administration. But as an organ of command, he could inform the commander about some things but not to report to him or to submit reports to him about his work. He didn't have to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: We'll come back to his reports to the corps commander in a few minutes. I want to go to what you've just said about the professional reporting line. The top of that for Colonel Lugonja, or the next step up, so to speak, would be General Tolimir at the VRS Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No. His superior was Beara because Beara was the chief of the security administration. His immediate superior was Beara, but the next superior up the chain was Tolimir, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. You referred to reporting that Colonel Lugonja may have done to the corps commander. Now, the corps commander during the time you were in the SRK was either General Milosevic or General Galic depending on the date; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And the corps commander held daily morning meetings with his command staff at which different units reported on the activities over the course of the past 12 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, I have to correct you in one part. The morning briefings at the corps commander were attended by the command organs of the corps; chiefs of the departments, the administrations, and so on. They were not attended by commanders of the units, operational units. Only the organs of command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Otherwise my description is accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sure. The corps commander held daily morning meetings, the staff that was present was as you just described, and that staff would report on the activities that had occurred during the past 12 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes. One correction regarding that as well. At that meeting, the organs of command would first of all be informed about the events over the previous 12 or 24 hours, but these meetings were held in the operations centre and that was an office, a room where all the data from the field would come in over the previous 24 hours. So at that morning meeting, all the organs of command had the opportunity to receive information about the current situation at the front, and in -- depending on the events or on the overall situation, they could plan their activities and possibly make proposals for some activities of our forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Are you saying, at the morning meetings, that the organs of command would both receive the information from their subordinates and report that information to the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Not submit reports. They would mostly receive assignments. I said depending on the situation and reports from the field that all came into the operations centre, the organs of the command, after certain analysis, would receive assignments in terms of planning possible activities on our part.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: We've spent a lot of time on what is a very simple question and, in fact, I'll just read to you some of your testimony from Galic so you can understand the basis of my question. This is at transcript page 18366 of your Galic testimony. "The way that the corps command worked, the commander made it an obligation to have a morning meeting, and this was an extensive meeting. Its objective was that the organs of the command learn about the situation on the front in the previous 12 hours of the previous night." Do you agree with your testimony? Can you please answer verbally for the record?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And you often --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, I'm a bit puzzled by page 29, line 14, where you talk about receive the information from their subordinates. It's not entirely clear to me how in that meeting those present would receive any information from their --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I was -- sorry, Mr. President. I was also unclear in my understanding of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you clarify it with the witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that would be most appropriate way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If you can give me one moment to look back at the source of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Colonel Bukva, you answered one of my questions, and this is at page 29 of the temporary transcript, starting around line 4, you answered that: "These meetings were held in the operations centre, and that was an office, a room where all the data from the field would come in over the previous 24 hours. So at that morning meeting, all the organs of command had the opportunity to receive information about the current situation at the front." So my question to you is: From whom were they receiving the information about the current situation at the front?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The information, in the form of regular combat reports, was received from regular units, from the brigades, and these regular daily combat reports would report on the situation at 1700 hours and the situation in the morning. So the brigade commands, yes, were obliged to submit regular combat reports which were all sent to the operations centre where the duty operations officer of the corps was. And he, in turn, would report to all the organs of the command about the situation on the basis of reports that he received from the units, from the brigades. He would compile one report and then would report or inform the organs of the command about the situation in the field. So I hope that I was clear. This would be done on the basis of reports that were coming in from the brigades, and these -- this information would be submitted at these morning briefings which were organised by the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This clarifies the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In the absence of Colonel Lugonja, as his deputy you would sometimes attend these meetings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: That is correct. As his deputy, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In the Galic trial you attended -- you testified that you attended 20 to 30 per cent of such meetings. Do you stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I do. That is a percentage that I am sure of, 20 to 30 per cent at the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm going to talk now -- ask a few questions about reports that were drafted by you or also by your colleagues in the intelligence unit -- intelligence department. Now, these written reports were required to follow a certain form; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Which reports are you thinking of? Could you please say that again for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Intelligence reports.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, they didn't have to be drafted in any specific format. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: For example, what would the first item of the report be about often?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I don't understand. I said that the reports that we were submitting to the superior in the professional sense didn't have any specific kind of form. I assume that you're thinking of combat reports that were being sent from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to the Main Staff. If that is your question, then, yes, I can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: No, but I do want to ask you about combat reports. Am I correct that you did not create combat reports?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, you are incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: One of your duties was to draft combat reports as opposed to intelligence reports?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No. Combat reports were drafted by the command and they were signed by the commander. That's a combat report. And that report has certain elements. The first item would be information about the enemy; the second item would be one's own forces and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I asked if you drafted combat reports. Based on the answer that you just gave, I understand that you did not.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now you've had an opportunity to review this statement in front of you. You've talked about several documents in that statement. All of them are combat reports; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: None of them are intelligence reports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Which document in your statement do you discuss that is an intelligence report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I don't think there are any. I believe there is only an order to subordinate units or, rather, subordinate organs. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, twice now where the question of the same structure, that is, a negative, and then to ask confirmation, it creates a confusion, apparently. Could you please keep this in mind when phrasing your next questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Moving back to the topic of intelligence reports. As an intelligence officer, you were tasked with providing high-quality information about anything that would impact the risk to the corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And earlier today when Mr. Lukic asked you about sources, you talked about a number of sources that you consulted, including listening to communications. Would you also speak to people that had come through from the Muslim-controlled parts of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I did so myself in a number of cases when such talks were of special interest or, rather, when the sources, the people who had crossed over to our territory from the Muslim side, had extremely interesting information that was useful to us. In such cases when we had an especially interesting source, I would talk to these people and my associates, such as Milidrag Lubura. But most of such cases were handled by our organs in brigades in the location where the person crossed over to our territory. For instance, if the person crossed over into the territory covered by the Ilidza Brigade, the case would be handled by our organ within the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This would include Serb civilians or Serb members of the armed forces who had come over from the Muslim-controlled sides; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Any person who would come over from the Muslim-controlled territory, including civilians and Serbs who had been mobilised by force and managed to escape at some point to territory under our control. But it was not only Serbs. Any person who had managed to leave Sarajevo or, rather, the part of the Sarajevo that was under Muslim control. There were convoys that exited Sarajevo legally, such as one that I remember, the convoy of Jews, of the Roma, et cetera. Only the Serbs did not have the right to leave Sarajevo, so there was no Serb convoy, and it was for understandable reasons because they were used as live -- human shields. And I remember another convoy, a convoy of Macedonians. Those were the three organised convoys that left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Earlier today at transcript page 11, this was in your testimony about using various sources for information, you included: "... conversations or interviews of people who switched to the other side." Can you just clarify -- sorry, it's not in your statement. It was from your testimony this morning. Do you need me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So I'm not referring to your statement. I'm referring to an answer that you gave this morning. You were talking about the sources of information and you referred to: "... conversations or interviews of people who switched to the other side." And my question is just what you are referring to with that phrase, "people that switched to the other side"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Maybe that's a little inconsistency, but it's implied that these people had crossed over to our side. We're talking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I could not be possibly interviewing people who had left our side to the other one. I could only talk to people who had come over to our side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. That does explain it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for one clarification as well. You said only the Serbs did not have the right to leave Sarajevo. Were the Muslims free to leave Sarajevo as they wished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no organised departure of Muslims from Sarajevo that I know. I mean, in convoys. I don't know why they would leave Sarajevo, but I know that they did leave based on the intelligence we had. And I have to say that, in doing so, they abused the Sarajevo airport which our forces had turned over to the UN force exclusively for humanitarian needs. Still, we had information that certain structures in Sarajevo - that is to say, the Muslims - were leaving for third countries using that airport. And another thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I stop you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there at this moment. You apparently make a distinction between organised departure and non-organised departure. When you talk about Muslims abusing the airport, was that because they had a right to leave or was this unauthorised departure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I wanted to clarify. The airport was abused insofar as, at the beginning, the Muslims were leaving across the runway illegally, and for the most part these were armed troops, armed Muslim troops. And again, later, at a certain point they built the tunnel under the runway with the entrance at Dobrinja and one exit at Donji Kotorac, and that's the way in which they abused the airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I go back to my initial question. You said Serbs were the only ones who were not allowed to leave. I take it that you were referring to Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now in general terms, were Muslim civilians free to leave as they wished, apart from at night crossing a runway or in very small numbers, perhaps, using a tunnel, but in general terms were Muslim civilians free to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the answer to that question. But it is a fact that there was not a single Muslim convoy that left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you said only the Serbs are not allowed to leave, that's not accurate in the sense that you do not know, as you told us now, whether Muslims were free to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My personal opinion is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- these two issues have nothing in common.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about your opinions. I'm asking you about facts. Please proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Returning to the issues of sources of intelligence. You had personnel along the front line who would monitor the activities of the enemy and report to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, my subordinates did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And you would monitor the media?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, you talked about how it wasn't just Serbs who you would interview for intelligence information. Did you also speak to non-Serbs that were captured by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No. For the most part, if you mean prisoners of war, these talks were conducted by our lower-level organs - that means organs in brigades - because the information in the possession of these persons was of most interest to brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You said before that if a brigade unit subordinate to you came across information that was important, that then you would speak to that person. So surely it's possible that a captured ABiH soldier would have information that was important from an intelligence perspective; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't quite clear. My section did that work but not me personally. I remember one case in particular. It was -- I can't remember the name of the person or the brigade. He was the intelligence organ in his brigade, and in a state of inebriation he crossed over into our territory and I interviewed him personally. That's the only case I can remember. I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'll refer you to your testimony --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Later on that man --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'll refer you to your testimony from temporary page 34. I asked you if you would speak to people that had come through from the Muslim-controlled parts of Sarajevo. Your answer, at line 34, line 8: "I did so on a number of cases when such talks were of special interest or, rather, when the sources, the people who had crossed over to our territory from the Muslim side, had extremely interesting information that was useful to us. In such cases when we had an especially interesting source, I would talk to these people and my associates," and then it continues to say most of the cases were handled by organs underneath -- in the brigades where they came in. So I understand you are saying mostly it was handled by the brigades, but you said yourself in a number of cases of special interest you would perform the interviews. So is that correct? If you can answer verbally for the record.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But that did not concern only prisoners of war. I said persons who had come in from the other side. It could be civilians, it could be prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So if at some point --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: But I clarified --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: At some point a prisoner of war would have information that would be of special interest to an intelligence section, is that not true? Actually, let me rephrase that. Is it true that a captured POW would have helpful intelligence information?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Well, that goes without saying. That's why I said that the brigades dealt with the bulk of that work. Why? Because the POW would be somebody from the vicinity of that brigade and he would have information about the forces facing that brigade, and it's logical that our brigade intelligence officer would conduct the interview, but sometimes somebody in the section would handle the interview. I just remembered this intelligence officer who wandered off into Grbavica and I talked to him for about ten minutes, seeking information that I was interested in at the time in a room designated for the purpose, not in the -- on the premises of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: When I ask you a question, if you can try to answer it accurately the first time, because this takes a lot of time. So, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, you introduced the most recent part of your questioning by referring to prisoners of war. That caused most of the confusion. We clearly see that we have information dealt with on the brigade level and by the level on which the witness functioned, and we have prisoners of war and those who crossed over. This is constantly going through another -- and in your questions, especially the last series of questions, you started by reference to the prisoners of war. That creates confusion. Not to say that the witness was in every respect always accurate, but apparently he's thinking in two different groups and two different levels, and an accurate phrasing of the question would have certainly avoided most of the confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The term "prisoner of war" actually came first from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, if I can just try to clarify what your evidence is. I asked you if you spoke to non-Serbs that were captured by the VRS, and your answer was: "No. For the most part, if you mean prisoners of war, these talks were conducted by our lower-level organs." So you can clarify for me if we're talking about -- let's talk first about prisoners of war. Did you sometimes conduct interviews of prisoners of war? If you can answer verbally for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I've already explained. Only in one case did I feel the need to interview such a prisoner myself, otherwise no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The bulk of that work was done by our brigade organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So is there a second category of persons, which I would describe as non-Serbs captured by the VRS, would you consider that to be a separate group from prisoners of war? For example, civilians.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Civilians, Serbs and Croats alike.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No. Muslim civilians did not cross over to our side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Here again there is a possible source of confusion. When you are talking about these civilians - as you said, Serbs and Croats alike - did you capture them when they crossed over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't say that we detained them, but when they crossed over it would be noticed and logically, since they were coming from enemy territory, they would be interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. That's -- that's a clear answer. Ms. MacGregor, I indeed misspoke. You started your line of questioning with persons captured --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then the witness apparently, immediately in his answer, understood people being captured as prisoners of war. And apparently here now there is a category, again, of people who were interviewed, crossed over, but were not captured and in that sense were no prisoners of war. And there is another, if I may give you some guidance on another matter as well, it may also be important to make a distinction between those dealt with at the brigade level and those dealt with at the witness's formation level but not necessarily be interviewed by him personally. That is still a distinction that may create some confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I think I will probably return to this topic when I have a chance to look over the past few pages of testimony. I'm going to continue with a new topic before we take the break, if that's okay, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's okay. We have another seven minutes to break time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: For the time being we're going to set aside the topic of what sources you consulted. I want to refer now to the topics that you were required to report about. So is it correct that you would collect intelligence on, for example, the number of personnel under the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I said any information that was of interest to our units. Anything that could pose a threat to our troops and civilians was interesting to us, including the strength of the enemy, the weaponry they had, their plans, deployment, movements, regrouping, all these things were directly linked to our interests.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did this include information about the morale of enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Combat morale. We were interested in the combat morale of the enemy army, their willingness to fight. Because, you see, there were a lot of incidents in their ranks, mutual clashes, internal clashes, and this information was of great importance to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You referred to the number of personnel as an example of information that you would collect. So, for example, if a VRS combat operation resulted in a loss of a significant number of personnel, would that be helpful intelligence to gather?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: By all means that information would be relevant to our estimates. It would be useful, but it was not of particular interest. We always received that information as part of our quest for other intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Why is it that a loss of a significant number of personnel would not be particularly interesting from an intelligence perspective?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I didn't say that we were not interested. I said that information would be obtained in pursuit of other interests. It was not a priority. It was useful but it was not our primary interest. Because there were far more important issues in which we were more interested. We were, for instance, more interested in how many troops were alive than dead, for instance, in a brigade that was facing us. It's much more important how much personnel, how much able-bodied fighting men they had. It was far more important than finding out their losses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Surely the amount of personnel alive is directly related to the amount that are killed in action for determining that intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I try to cut this short. Apparently the issue you want to raise and the issue you are questioned about, Mr. Bukva, is that you are interested in the strength, personnel strength of the troops. And, of course, if a significant number of the troops would die, then a smaller number would remain but could be completed with others, I take it. And therefore you're emphasizing that you'd like to know how many troops remained at the end after losses, after completion, et cetera, rather than the exact number of people who had died in an operation. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, roughly. That's a good understanding. For our purposes, far more important is the information of combat-ready personnel. The information about losses could be interesting but not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are a lot of -- Ms. MacGregor, there are a lot of implied assumptions in there. That is that if troops -- if a significant number dies, that you would know in advance how many there are, so therefore how many remain, and that they would not be completed, et cetera. There is a lot of implied assumptions which, I think, the witness constantly has on its mind and which you have not made explicit by yourself and that creates perhaps here and there the -- the talk on not fully understanding each other. Please proceed. But when I say "please proceed," it is time for a break. Mr. Bukva, if you would follow the usher. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to start with the associated exhibits which I'd forgotten before the break, or at least there was no time left. Mr. Lukic, could you briefly mention the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's 1D319.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1D00319 receives, Madam Registrar, number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D00319 receives D609.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D609 is admitted. Next one, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D2969 receives D610.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that I think our staff -- it was not easy to get access to the translation. Is there no translation? No translation issue if I understand well. Next one -- let me see. D610 is admitted. Next one, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next one is 1D02970.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D02970 receives D611.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next one is 1D02971.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D02971 receives D612.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. And then, I think, the map marked by the witness is the remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And it's a corrected number. It's 1D3093.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D03093 receives D613.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D613 is admitted into evidence. As far as the map is concerned, I noticed that in e-court there is no translation, even not for the small portions of text which appear on the map. Most of it has been properly explained, perhaps not every single word. It seems that there is some reference to mortars, for example, 120-millimetre mortars, which I do not understand because it's written on a place, could be mobile mortars, could be anything. But could you please check, Mr. Lukic, together with the Prosecution, whether you are satisfied with the -- whether both parties are satisfied with the text and the accessibility of that text to the parties and therefore to the Bench as well. Then meanwhile the witness can be escorted into the courtroom. Two observations. Mr. Lukic, perhaps it's -- there is no need to draw your attention to the fact that the Chamber is always best assisted, if it comes to protective measures, and I have specifically in mind at this moment the request for protective measures of -- oh, I'm sorry. I -- I would have to move in private session. I'll do that later today. I've said nothing, I think, which could -- needs any redaction. Then, Ms. MacGregor, we heard a lot of questions and are all rather general and vague. If you could come to your point so that we know exactly what the relevance of all of it is, apart from knowing the structure. Of course, knowing the structure is not unimportant but it's -- we would like to see you to come to your point as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If, while we're waiting for the witness, we could have Exhibit P4900 come up, that may save some time, and we'll be looking first at the fist pages in both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, you previously asked when we would have a response to the videolink. We'll have that filed no later than tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's appreciated. The same, by the way, Mr. Lukic, is true for the examination-in-chief. Vague and general statements, answers such as: The Serbs never thought about the war. I mean, that's -- that's not easy to test that or perhaps very easy to test that, I do not know, but it's not of great assistance to the Chamber to have these general statements --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- rather than concrete matters which, of course, the Chamber is primarily interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I -- as I remember, I just asked about cease-fires and the witness added this. So it was not part of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But statements like: Most of the cease-fires were violated by, then I think the Chamber would very much appreciate to have one cease-fire violated so that it can be tested by the other party as well, whether it really -- whether the perception of the witness of such a violation is accurate and -- rather than general sweeping statements about violation of cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that in these documents we can find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- cease-fires that are not followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.
