utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And according to the statements, it's the other side to be blamed for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. Then we reached, then, a more concrete level. Ms. MacGregor, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Colonel Bukva, if you see on the screen in front of you, on the left side of the screen in the B/C/S language, do you see the rules of service for military security organs. And do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Does this document outline the rules for the work of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can please turn to page, in the English, 13, in the B/C/S, 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: We're going to look now at chapter 3, paragraph 29. In this paragraph there is a reference to security organs conducting counter-intelligence evaluation. Can you please tell the Chamber what is meant by "counter-intelligence evaluation"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see "counter-intelligence" in paragraph 29, unless there is a part of it I don't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sorry. You're right. It's paragraph 27, a little bit further up on the English and hopefully on the same -- it may need to go -- yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Colonel Bukva, do you see the reference to "counter-intelligence evaluation" that we're discussing? I see that you're nodding. Can you just explain what your understanding of --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: What's your understanding of that term?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Counter-intelligence evaluation is a thought process in the work of the intelligence and security organs. It's one of the tasks of the security organs. It's done on the basis of gathered intelligence data, and its objective is, on the basis of the evaluation of the intelligence, to propose measures that lead to the prevention of intelligence threats to one's own forces. So a counter-intelligence evaluation could be in the form of a document, but actually it's a continuing, ongoing thought process of intelligence organs that alters depending on the situation in the field. If I have been clear. The security organ at any point in time must have a proposal for solutions for a specific situation in keeping with the intelligence that is available to it on the basis of its intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Is counter-intelligence evaluation a thought process that you applied in your intelligence gathering -- one of the thought processes that you applied?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, no. It states here clearly that security organs -- intelligence organs, that's a different category. These are two separate organs that in principle function for the same objectives. Security organs, on the basis of intelligence data that we prepare for them and other information available to us, conduct this process of counter-intelligence evaluation and propose to the command organs prevention measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: We can take this document from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Colonel Bukva, I'm now going to turn to your evidence about the locations of ABiH and VRS forces in Sarajevo during the war. In paragraph 18 of your statement, you discuss specifics about the personnel strength of the ABiH, and you state that the ABiH had 38.000 armed soldiers in Sarajevo. Now, you testified in the Galic trial that the ABiH had 35.000 to 38.000 armed men. Is your Galic testimony accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, correct, on the basis of information that was available to us at the time. This figure corresponded to the actual figures, the number of men under -- carrying weapons in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Can you repeat the number -- can you please repeat the number you just provided in your last answer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I said based on information that we had at the time, the number over the four-year period varied, but it ranged from 35.000 to 38.000 armed soldiers in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You testified in the Galic trial, and this is at transcript 18364, lines 4 through 11, I'm going to read an excerpt from that testimony. "I said at the beginning that in the city itself there were about 38.000 armed troops. Out of that there were 30.300 or, let's say, 31.000 were in the BH Army units -- were part of the BH Army units. And several special units, special MUP units also existed in Sarajevo, in the part of the Sarajevo under Muslim control. We assessed that these troops amounted to the strength of one brigade." Is it correct that approximately of the 35- to 38.000 that you've referred to, is it correct that 31.000 were in fact in the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Again, I say that the number varied. In any event, according to our estimate, it -- our estimate was what I just referred to, and we operated on the basis of the assumption that these figures were accurate figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Were between 4- and 7.000 of those personnel in fact members of special MUP units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If you could please take a look at paragraph 23 of your statement. Now, the second sentence of this statement -- excuse me, this paragraph, you talk about the location of the command post of the 105th Light Infantry Brigade at Bistrik.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, if you look at paragraph 24 you -- in the third sentence of that paragraph, you talk about the position of the 115th Brigade positioned at Bistrik. So I just wanted to clarify with you: Are both of these references correct or should they both be referring to the 115th Light Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Right. Actually, the command posts of both of these brigades were at Bistrik, the 105th and the 115th Brigade. At Bistrik, that was the higher command of the 4th Corps -- actually, that was the location of the former 4th JNA Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In a moment we'll have an opportunity to look at the map that you marked in the Galic trial and then we'll return to this topic. Now, in paragraph 21 of your statement you state that the ABiH had heavy weaponry positioned at Zlatiste. Now, Zlatiste was actually held by the VRS, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: When you refer to Zlatiste, can you just describe where that is in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: That is - how can I explain it to you? - it's at Mount Trebevic below -- in any event, it's a location at Trebevic, let's say, roughly above -- above Skenderija. Perhaps a better orientation point would be the Olympic venue. I think that the Olympic venue for the bob-trail was below it. So Zlatiste is there --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Let's look at --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: -- near that Olympic bob-trail.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we could look at D613, page 2 of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This is the map that you marked in the Galic case. We're going to look at the east side of Sarajevo on this map. And if you like, we can just have one page up on the screen so that it's bigger, the east side of the map. Page 2. Okay. So, sir, if I can direct your attention slightly to the right middle are the words in red "Stari Grad." Now, I see the word "Zlatiste" to the south-west of Stari Grad. Do you see where I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we enlarge it a bit further for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then including the word "Zlatiste," I would suggest. That is further down. Could we zoom out again. Could we move to the lower part of the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I also have a hard copy that I could provide to the witness if that would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think at this moment we can clearly see it on the screen. Witness, do you see the words "Zlatiste" which seems to be below the yellow road lowest on the map, which may well be the Pale-Lukavica road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I do see it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And is the location on this map consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Could you please reformulate the question? What do you mean, "according to your recollection"?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Does this map seem accurate to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, this is a map of the Sarajevo city.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can zoom out again and, in fact, show both sides of the map, east and west. I'm also going to ask if the court usher can provide this hard copy of the map to the witness. It may assist when we're looking at multiple places at the same time. I do have one hard, colour copy as well extra if it would assist the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at Zlatiste on the map that you marked in the Galic case, you see that you have not marked at Zlatiste the 112th Vitez Motorised Brigade. In fact, you've marked the 112th Vitez Motorised Brigade on page 1 of the map.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, that is the Boljakov Potok sector. Boljakov Potok. There is one thing that is creating confusion here. According to what I know, one area in this section has a similar name, Zlatiste or something like that. In any event, what is being discussed here is this area here, not Zlatiste in any case because at that point Zlatiste was on our side. We were controlling the area that was on this side of the road. So this is an inconsistency here, because the location that I am speaking of is the one that is marked. So in terms of the name, geographically, Boljakov Potok is where I indicated the heavy weaponry of the 112th Vitez Brigade is there. There is a location that has a similar name, so it's possible that there is some confusion here because of that. So it is not in the area that we're looking at here on this side, the area with the name of Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I think now that the matter has been clarified on the record, that there are two places that have the name Zlatiste.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can please look --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Same or similar. Or similar. And that's how it's been recorded in the transcript, as Zlatiste. It could be that but it could be similar. I mean, it's been a long time since then, so I cannot remember the precise name.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: On the eastern side of the map --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And for e-court, we can just look at the eastern side for this question so it will be bigger.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If you focus on approximately the centre of the map to the right, you'll see where you've marked the 115th Brigade. There is what looks to me two places where you marked the number 115. Do you see those locations? It's blown up as well on this --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Do you see that --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- between those numbers, 115 and 115, on the map the area of Bistrik is marked? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now looking over to your left and up a bit, we see a flag with the number 105 in it. Now, I return again to my question about the location of the 105th versus the 115th. From this map they do not appear to both be in Bistrik, but what is your testimony about their location?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The point is the command of this brigade was in Bistrik, but the whole unit was based in this installation marked by a flag inside which "105 Pbr" is written. That's where the whole unit -- the actual unit was. But the command post was in Bistrik.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: The command post of which brigade was in Bistrik?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The 105th Brigade. Its command post was in Bistrik. But this is an inconsistency. The place marked by the flag marks the location of the unit, the whole unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So you have not marked the location of the 105th Brigade command post on this map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: You noticed that well. It's an inconsistency, indeed. But the information is correct. The flag should have been in Bistrik. Instead, I marked the actual place of deployment of the unit. I made a mistake. This is not the command post but the unit, whereas the command post was in Bistrik together with the 115th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness one clarification. We see these little flags in the map. Sometimes at the bottom of the flag there is a small triangle, sometimes there is a small circle. Could you tell us first what a flag with a small triangle stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I almost have forgotten these topographic designations and how units should be marked. The triangle with a flag that is rhomboid is a designation for a brigade. A circle with a triangular flag marks a battalion, I believe. The command post of a battalion. For instance, the triangular flag in a circle is a battalion command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could you then explain to us. You see the lowest marking in the map with a text attached to it, which seems to refer to a school, see you -- do see that? It's just above the word "Stari Grad" at this moment at the very lower part of the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stari Grad, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's at Hrid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just above that. Do you see handwritten text? Two words, the second apparently being "skola"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a primary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there is a line between that text to a flag which is just above it with a circle at the bottom and then a triangular flag above it. Could you tell us exactly what that indicates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Inside the flag we see "1/115." That's the 1st Battalion of the 115th Brigade. It was deployed in a primary school in a part of town called Hrid. 1 means the 1st Battalion, slash 115, meaning from the 115th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. May I seek one more clarification to better understand how certain items are referred to. Do you see -- in the centre of this map, do you see "GS KM" in a square box?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see it. It says "GS" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Is that -- what does GS stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a rectangular flag with a line -- two lines inside. GS means Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And below that, we see KM and that was the command post of the Main Staff of the BH Army, and it was inside the building of the Presidency of the BH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I -- it seems that there is a line between the bottom of this rectangular flag to a triangle which is a little bit further to the left, just left below where it reads "100-112," do you see that little triangle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What does that triangle stand for? Is that the -- how is that linked to any of the text in flags?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are linked by this line. This triangle is part of the flag. But to make the picture more understandable, that's how we draw the sign. Whereas the triangle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that the triangle indicates the location where the Main Staff was situated and that is depicted by a line with a -- linking this square flag to that little triangle. My last question is: The 100-112 reference stands for what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see a triangular flag here and inside it -- and in its base is a circle. Next to it we read "KM." This is not "100," it's "IDO," that means reconnaissance sabotage detachment, slash 112, that's the number of the brigade from which this detachment came. So this is a command post and the unit was deployed in the same place. Daniel Ozma Street number 7, I believe. That's where this reconnaissance sabotage detachment of the 112th Brigade was deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my questions. Mr. Lukic, this is exactly the type of information which one would expect in a legend, or perhaps you could agree on the basis of the evidence of the witness what the legend would be for this map and the translation for it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can please have in e-court 08282B, as in boy. Also, if I could ask the court usher to bring the hard copy of the map and place it on the easel. Your Honours, this map is very difficult to see in e-court. I've made colour copies for each of you and also for the Defence. Unfortunately, the very best copy is the copy that the witness will be looking at.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record the document is Exhibit P2952.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Colonel Bukva, the map that's being placed next to you is a map of the ABiH. It's dated 15 March 1995. I'm going to be asking you to look at that map and to compare something with the map that you marked in the Galic trial. So in a moment I'll ask you to get up and have a look at the map. I'll remind you that while you're pointing at the map and far away from the microphone, it will be hard to record your answers so if you can wait a moment before you head over there so I can explain to you what we'll be looking at. Okay. Do you see on the right-hand side of the map that there are numbers marking the grids? At this point you can just nod if you want to let me know that you understand. On the very right-hand side of the map there is handwritten numbers.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: You mean these numbers?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Correct. And there are similar numbers along the bottom of the grid -- excuse me, along the bottom of the map. Do you see those numbers? I see that you're pointing to them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness was first pointing to the numbers 52 to 62 at the right-hand side of the map, and then later to the numbers at the bottom ranging from 23 to 40. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look on that map where the 102nd Brigade is marked, and I'll give you some guidance. If you look at the grid between -- I'll start on the right-hand side, it's between 56 and 55, at that particular row. And then if you go over to the left, looking along the bottom, between numbers 26 and 27.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have circled in red on the hard copies that you have the flag that I'm going to be asking the witness about, and also for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Colonel Bukva, do you see there in that square a flag with the marking -- excuse me, with the number 102?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay. Now keeping your eye on that to orient us, two grid squares to the right are four oval shapes that mark the neighbourhood of Alipasino Polje. Are you able to locate that neighbourhood? It's in the same row between bottom map grid numbers 28 and 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I can confirm that the witness was pointing with his pointer directly to these four ovals.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And I see that the witness is also nodding.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If you -- you can have a seat again so that you can look at your own map. Now, I'm going to ask you on your own map, on page 1 of that map, to look at where you've marked the 102nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In e-court if we can please have D613, page 1. It's approximately in the middle of that page. Okay. That perspective is good.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Witness, do you see, either on the screen or in the hard copy in front of you, where you've marked the 102nd?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, if you again look for the neighbourhood of Alipasino Polje, you'll see that you've marked the 102nd Brigade almost directly above that neighbourhood. Do you agree with that description?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So you've marked it much further west -- excuse me, much further east on your map than the marking on the ABiH map of this same brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: The command post of the 102nd Infantry Brigade, according to our information, was in the wire factory at Alipasin Bridge. You can see here Alipasin Most, bridge. This is -- could I look again at your map? The command of the BH Army. There is a difference but I still maintain that this information -- this data is from 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: According on the date on the map, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: This is certainly the data that we had. At that moment it was correct. Especially because right next to the command post of the 102nd Brigade was an ammunition plant. It's possible it moved for security reasons. It happened during the war, command posts were relocated because there was always a danger they would be detected and exposed to artillery and other fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: According to this, according to their map, their MAD, mixed artillery battalion, was in this location, if you look at the map that I drew. So it's possible that this command post moved to what was earlier the command post of their mixed artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I believe you're referring to the MAD that you marked on your map on the -- is that correct? The one that is slightly to the left and above the 102 --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: But even that flag where it says "MAD" is still significantly further east than the location marked 102 on the ABiH map; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: I repeat: For the reasons I described, it's possible they changed the location of their command post. It wouldn't be unusual. But for us, the location of the wire factory at Alipasin Bridge was the identified command post of the 102nd Brigade at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay. You've referenced just now that at times command posts would relocate or reorganise because of strategic advantages or other reasons. Is it correct that intelligence on where enemy forces were located is specifically relevant only when you know the certain date of that intelligence? And I'm not sure if I've asked that in a confusing way. Let me ask it this way: If I asked you where something was located, is it correct that your answer might change depending on what date I was asking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: You're right. It's a variable, and movements on the front line are a regular occurrence. For instance, if we had some artillery in one firing positions and the situation requires that they be moved, our prior information would no longer be correct. Units move and positions move. All elements of a combat disposition are in a certain juxtaposition at one moment and in a different juxtaposition at a different moment. The brigade would redeploy its units and move them from one theatre of war to another, from one part of the front line to another.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So in your statement --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: That's why this is a complex matter. It has to be followed constantly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So in your statement in paragraphs 20 through 27, you describe very specific locations of ABiH forces and weaponry, but you don't include any dates as to what -- as to when this intelligence would be accurate. So as you've described it in your statement, it's difficult to verify where things are located without a date; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. This data relates to the period when the corps was under the command of General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that still is quite a period of time, isn't it? If you say they move from one place to another, that could have been done during the tenure of General Galic as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] As I understand it, the map -- the ABiH map is already in evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. As I understand it, the ABiH map is already in evidence, so I won't be moving that into evidence. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is one issue, Ms. MacGregor. You gave us a marked version to look at and I take it that the copy in evidence is not the marked version. Therefore, it's important that we know exactly what you marked for us and what we looked at, which is, I would say, one of the few clear flags on that map.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps it would be best if you enlarge the relevant portion, including the Alipasino Polje area, and tender that into evidence so that it's later possible to know what we looked at and what we compared as far as positions are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a suggestion that you tender again the same map with your marking and on -- at page 2, an extract of that map which more clearly indicates exactly where that marking is in relation to the surrounding -- surrounding buildings and streets, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And if it's all right with the Chamber, I'll work on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- on a break and get back to you. I think unfortunately when it's zoomed in on e-court, it is very, very difficult to see. So I think Judge Fluegge's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I did that, and it certainly gives a better indication than just without. At least it's clear where the flag is. It's also clear where Alipasino Polje is, so it gives a better opportunity to get an impression of where that flag exactly is located.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If Your Honours have an opportunity to look at the hard copy, it actually is incredibly much easier to see everything on that map than -- than you would guess from the e-court version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I tend to disagree, but we have them both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam MacGregor, if I might just ask a question. Am I correct to say that in fact that flag we are talking about you associate with the 102nd Light Brigade, and I thought you said that 102 is -- can be seen on the map here, and I would like you to show it to me if you can, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If you give me a moment just to review your question, Your Honour. The 102nd can be seen on the large map in the location -- the large ABiH map in the location where I've placed a red circle on the hard copy which I've provided to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What just -- can we see there, is there an indication of 102? Can we read something that makes that flag or is it --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: On the hard map next to the witness, yes, you can. On the version that you have, I certainly can't read "102" in there. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Our eyes may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's just below the flag itself, a little bit to the right. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I actually think it's inside the triangle of the flag, Your Honour. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You can't see anything on the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly why we have difficulties. Could we again have Exhibit - what was it? - 2959 -- 2952 on our screens. And could we enlarge on where the flag appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, further down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Much further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Much further down. To the left. To the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where now can we --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: A little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- see the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: A little north-west of centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I see where it is, but I would like to read the "102" somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Again, it's inside the flag. At this level you won't be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: It is on the hard copy of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you explain, Ms. MacGregor, the number below the flag, a little bit to the right?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break now, and the Chamber would like to have an opportunity to look at the map which is in the courtroom at this moment so as to know for sure whether we really -- we find 102 just -- what seems to us to be just below the flag rather than in the flag itself. We would like to have an opportunity to do that. But we first invite the witness to follow the usher and be back with us in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, but most likely the Chamber will first have a look at the map but does that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If we leave the courtroom, if then we would find an empty courtroom in two or three minutes after that, then we have a look at the map. And we resume at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, needless to say that in addition to what I said in private session, of course, the Chamber always gives an opportunity to further explore any reasons for any such request and only decides after it has heard all that. Then the witness can be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I put on the record that the Chamber during the break had a look at the map which is now in the courtroom and which we have looked at under number P2952. And on the original from which the -- from which the e-court version is scanned, it is clear that the flag the Prosecution has drawn our attention to, in the flag itself the numbers 102 are clearly visible, whereas immediately below the flag, at the bottom of the flag, there is a clear reference to the 102nd Light Infantry Brigade. I put that hereby on the record. If the parties would disagree on it, the Chamber would like to know that without delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And as the suggestion or at least a request to upload an extract of the map so that we know exactly what flag you have drawn our attention to, because there are more flags on that map, is still standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And we won't be using the map anymore. I don't know if it needs to remain on the easel or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can leave it where it is --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If I can please have Prosecution Exhibit P4900 in e-court; specifically, page 21 of the English version and page 17 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: While we wait for that to come to the screen, Colonel Bukva, I'm again going to show you the document that we looked at before, the rules of service for military security organs. We're going to focus on chapter 5, a few paragraphs in this chapter. And the title of the chapter 5, as you see hopefully on your screen now, is: "The Operational Procedure of Security Organs in Criminal Procedure." I draw your attention to paragraph 52.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: It may help to enlarge the B/C/S left-hand side of the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Now, I read from paragraph 52: "When there are reasonable grounds to suspect that a crime within a security organ's competence has been committed ..." Now stopping there, can you explain for the Chamber what types of crime would fall under a security organ's competence as referred to here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Perhaps I won't remember all of them that are listed in that law, but first of all, I just need to remind you that these rules of the security service applied to peacetime conditions and it was taken over from the former JNA. In the rules of the procedure of the JNA, it is stated, among other things, that crimes - and here we're talking about crimes committed against the armed forces - are those crimes which jeopardise the security -- the personal security and the property of the armed forces. To be clear, once again, I have read the whole paragraph, what is being discussed here are crimes that are perpetrated against members of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You've said -- you said these rules were the rules of the former JNA, and is -- is it correct that the VRS, for the most part, adopted these rules?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Like I said, this rule was taken from the JNA. And it applied to peacetime conditions. Since Republika Srpska never proclaimed a state of war, we operated according to the peacetime rules. So this article was in force in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And it was in force during the years of the war, even though technically the VRS had not declared a war. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Republika Srpska never declared a state of war, not the VRS. The assembly is the one that declares a state of war as the supreme organ of power. Since this did not happen in Republika Srpska, then the Army of Republika Srpska operated according to peacetime rules, and the security services, accordingly, operated to this rule which had been inherited from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Continuing with paragraph 52 where we left off: "... authorised officers of the security organ are obliged the take necessary measures to ensure that the perpetrator of a crime is found, that the perpetrator or accomplice does not go into hiding or escape, that traces of the crime and objects that may serve as evidence are discovered and secured, and also that all information that may be of use for the successful pursuit of criminal proceedings is gathered." Is that description consistent with your understanding of your obligations during your time at the SRK intelligence department?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Here we're talking about the obligations of the security organs, and this is a completely different area which doesn't have anything in common with the intelligence organs. So this paragraph does not refer to intelligence organs. And in the heading of the chapter it states: "The Operational Procedure of Security Organs in Criminal Procedure." So they did have some duties in relation to investigative procedures, but intelligence organs did not do any such jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: So you were not required to, for example, ensure that necessary -- excuse me, to take necessary measures to ensure that a perpetrator of a crime is found?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: That does not -- that is not stated in the law. The law did not oblige us to do that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your focused on the use of the word "security" -- excuse me, the phrase "security organs" at the top of the chapter. I'd like to look a little bit more into how this manual defines that term so that we can better understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can please look at paragraph 2. This is both e-court and English -- excuse me, both English and B/C/S e-court page 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: We're going to look now at a chapter that's called: "Competence and Tasks of Security Organs." Would you agree with me this, again, only refers to security organs and not to intelligence organs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: That is correct. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 2, there is a reference to detecting and preventing activities aimed against the armed forces and the preparations of the armed forces for the country's defence. Now, your job was to detect information that would put the SRK at risk; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can please look at paragraph 6(b). It's on the same page in the B/C/S but on the next page on the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'll read again: "Security organs are responsible for the detection, tracking, and prevention of hostile activities by individuals, groups, or organisations against the armed forces and members of the armed forces ..." Now, would you agree that your job included the detection, tracking, and prevention of those hostile activities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: What is written in the paragraph refers to counter-intelligence activities which are conducted by the security organs and organs of the military police. So these are counter-intelligence activities whose purpose is to prevent the endangerment of units of the JNA or, in this case, units of the VRS. This --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Where do you see the reference --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: -- did not apply. You need to differentiate between security work and intelligence work which has a completely different function.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I understand. I'm attempting to do that. I don't see a reference in paragraph 6(b) to counter-intelligence work. Can you show us where that is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counter-intelligence is, according to the witness's evidence, is the function of security; therefore, this topic here relates to counter-intelligence because it's for security. In --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may ask him about this. The entire manual is actually referring to security organs and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- then I'd like to ask his understanding of the term.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I ask again: Is there a specific reference to counter-intelligence in paragraph 6(b)?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry. We have it in the title. It says: "Security organs should carry next tasks." So it says "security organs," so it creates only confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- but I think the issue is whether it says anywhere "counter-intelligence" because that was part of the witness -- his answers. I give an opportunity to Ms. MacGregor to further explore.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: There are two issues I'm trying to explore with you, Colonel Bukva. So let's start with the issue of -- you have described paragraph 6(b) as referring to counter-intelligence activities. Can you explain why you believe 6(b) is only referring to counter-intelligence activities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: It's not just 6(b) that refers to counter-intelligence activities. Generally, all functions of the security organs could be referred to by a single name and that would be counter-intelligence, protection of units and institutions of the Army of Republika Srpska. Protection from threats from the opposite side, coming from the enemy side. So under one name, all measures that intelligence or security organs undertake are counter-intelligence activities. These are preventative measures, organisational measures, all types of measures undertaken by security organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: In your answer you've just said that: "... under one name, all measures that intelligence or security organs undertake are counter-intelligence activities." And then you said: "These are preventative measures, organisational measures, all types of measures undertaken by security organs." So those two sentences are slightly different. The first sentence implies that intelligence organs undertake counter-intelligence activities. Do intelligence organs undertake counter-intelligence activities as you understand that term?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, no, you misunderstood me. Intelligence organs do not carry our counter-intelligence measures. Counter-intelligence measures are the result of the work and of the evaluation of the situation, the results of information that is gathered and evaluation of the situation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, could you please slow down and could you resume your answer by where you said: "... the results of information that is gathered and evaluation of the situation ..." And could you resume from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On the basis of intelligence information gathered and the conclusions on the basis of an evaluation of the situation, security organs propose measures of a preventive nature, organisation and technical nature or any other nature whose objective is to neutralise negative influences or effects on the units of the Army of Republika Srpska which would be coming from the enemy's side.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You seem to be emphasizing right now that only the security organs were involved in counter-intelligence evaluation. And I refer you to your testimony earlier today at temporary page 49, where I ask you about the reference to counter-intelligence evaluation in paragraph 29 of this same document. Your answer, starting at line 19 on page 49, is as follows: "Counter-intelligence evaluation is a thought process in the work of the intelligence and security organs. It's one of the tasks of the security organs." So I may be misunderstanding you but there are at least two times where you have referred to counter-intelligence work as being a task of both the security organ and the intelligence organ. So can you please clarify if it is, in fact, a role that both types of organs undertake?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: No, it's a misunderstanding, and I apologise if I'm the one who's responsible for that, but I state decisively the following. I repeat: Intelligence organs work on intelligence and that has nothing to do with counter-intelligence. That work has nothing to do with counter-intelligence work. As for the security organs, and I said that when I speak about the counter-intelligence evaluation that is the basic method of work of the security organs, exclusively the security organs. So I don't know how this misunderstanding came about. So the main method of work of security organs is counter-intelligence, and I said that it's a thought process that goes on continuously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, you should perhaps make a distinction between counter-intelligence and counter-intelligence evaluation. Counter-intelligence is not the same as counter-intelligence evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I understand what your point is, Your Honour. I will go back through the testimony. I believe that it hasn't been that clear as a distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could I --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just try to seek some clarity. Let me just try to tell you how I understood your testimony in this respect and if could you then perhaps either confirm or say that I understood it all wrong. I do understand that intelligence is collecting all kind of information which -- especially about enemy forces, which is relevant for any operational decision-making process. Is that more or less well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in principle, yes, that is well understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I understand counter-intelligence to be the activity to undermine the intelligence of the opposing armed forces; that is, either to block their sources of information or to prevent them from learning secret information from your armed forces. And I also understood that you said gathering information about the enemy, intelligence, was the task of the intelligence service; whereas undermining, blocking, frustrating, the intelligence of the opponent armed forces was the task of the security unit. That is how I more or less understood your testimony. Is that well understood or do you say no, you're totally wrong in understanding my testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have understood it excellently, precisely as it should be understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I start blushing, Ms. MacGregor will continue her examination -- her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] If we can go back, then, to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If we can return to paragraph 6(b).

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: This part I read to you is as follows: "Security organs are responsible for the detection, tracking, and prevention of hostile activities by individuals, groups or organisations against the armed forces or members of the armed forces." Would you agree that your role included the detection and tracking of such information?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that was 6(a).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: It's, if you look at 6(b), the detection and prevention -- oh, I -- sorry, yes. With the word "tracking." Can you look, Mr. Witness, at paragraph 6(a). I'll read again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you to Judge Fluegge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: "The detection, tracking, and prevention of intelligence activities ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Actually, I'm sorry. I am sticking to 6(b) but removing the word "tracking" and that -- I see where the confusion is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Colonel Bukva, were you responsible for the detection of hostile activities by individuals, groups or organisations against the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Well, your question seems to indicate again that the gist has been misunderstood. No. Intelligence work is directed towards the enemy, not towards one's own forces. What you're talking about, 6(b), is the work of the security organs, exclusively the work of security organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Do you agree that the title of this manual is: "The Rules of Service for Military Security Organs," the entire manual?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think that is what it says on the cover of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And you testified --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA
utterances.text: These are the rules of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And you testified this morning that these were the rules that outlined your obligations as part of the intelligence organ?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. I wanted to object before. Now you have -- at page 49, the question was put in reference of security organs. Not intelligence organs. And all the answers were in connection to security organs, when first it was [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you want to say that it misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are separate rules for his service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was a ruling, Mr. Lukic. The objection is granted. Please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the objection. I'm referring to testimony that this witness gave earlier when we referred to this document, much earlier. The first time we looked at this document. And I can find the reference if you like. I see that we're past the time for the end of the day, but I'm not referring to the testimony he just gave just a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then -- yes, what I should have done, as a matter of fact, is I should have given you an opportunity to respond. Where are you referring to if not to page 49?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 49, line 3. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not a couple of minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But -- no, Ms. MacGregor has an opportunity to indicate where she is referring to if it is different from what Mr. Lukic referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I will have found it in a moment if you grant me just a small dispensation. Okay. Sorry. Okay. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- you found it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes. I am at transcript page 48. And this is when I first showed Colonel Bukva this document. And at line 24, I asked: "Does this document outline the rules for the work of your unit?" And he answered: "Yes." And that is the question -- that is the answer that I was questioning him about at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And your next question makes clear that this paragraph, there is a reference to security organs conducting counter-intelligence evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, the next question which is specifically about paragraph 28. The point I'm getting at is that the entire manual is entitled -- is directed towards security organs. That's the only point I'm trying to get across, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There is no dispute in that respect. It all is about security organs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And he's testified that the manual did apply to his work. I just trying to confirm that. That's all I'm actually trying to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I think what he's trying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: His unit. "If this document outlines the rules of the work for your unit." That was your question. What do -- that was very unclear. Which unit did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Shall I -- I'll put the question to him with more specificity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you please -- if you further want to explore the matter, irrespective of whether that is -- will greatly assist the Chamber, then perhaps the way in which it was organised - that is, which tasks were put together in what kind of units and what these tasks exactly were, security, intelligence - should be clearly distinguished. The organisational aspect is not the same as the functional aspect in terms of task. Could you please keep that in mind. I'll leave it to you whether you want to further explore the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I would just have one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please put that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then that's -- yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have no -- yes, yes. It's time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. That's what I meant, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But is this a withdrawal only for the day or for the week, to say so?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I have further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But not that one question you had on your mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm going to take the opportunity to think on it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's always very wise. I think everyone would agree with that. Mr. Bukva, we'll adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom, II. And I inform the parties that we are more or less condemned to stay in this courtroom II for the rest of the week, the technical problems not having overcome yet. But before you follow the usher, Mr. Bukva, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way to whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given today or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that's clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, in terms of time, where are we?

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I believe -- I believe I've used just over half of my time, and I intend to finish tomorrow, probably not in the first section -- session but in the second session. I would imagine I have about an hour to an hour and a half more of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that's clear to us. We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 2nd of September, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
